t.2.35.2: Having taken leave of him as well, the righteous Rāghava, together with Sītā, bewildered by grief, saluted his mother.
t.2.35.1: Then Rāma and Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa with his palms joined in reverence, clasped the feet of the king and, full of sorrow, walked around him keeping him to their right.
t.2.35.3: Right after his brother, Lakṣmaṇa paid his respects to Kausalyā; then he clasped once more the feet of his mother Sumitrā.
t.2.35.4: As the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, bowed before her, his mother, weeping and wishing for his welfare, kissed him on the head and spoke to him.
t.2.35.5: You have been sent forth to dwell in the forest, deeply devoted as you are to the one you love. My son, do not be heedless toward Rāma as your brother goes.
t.2.35.6: Whether he is in misfortune or in prosperity, he is your refuge, O sinless one. This is the dharma of the good in the world: that one should remain obedient to one's elder brother.
t.2.35.7: For this is the fitting and eternal conduct of this family: giving gifts, undertaking consecration at sacrifices, and laying down one's body in battles.
t.2.35.9: Then Sumantra, humble and versed in courtesy, with joined palms addressed these words to Kākutstha, as Mātali addresses Vāsava.
t.2.35.8: Regard Rāma as Daśaratha, regard Janaka's daughter as me, and regard the forest as Ayodhyā. Go, my dear son, and fare happily.
t.2.35.10: Mount the chariot, may good fortune be yours, O prince of great renown! Quickly I shall bring you wherever you tell me, O Rāma.
t.2.35.11: For fourteen years you must dwell in the forest; you must begin those years, the ones the queen has urged upon you.
t.2.35.12: Sītā, of beautiful hips, having adorned herself, mounted with a joyful heart that chariot which shone like the sun.
t.2.35.13: Likewise, the two brothers placed on the floor of the chariot their many weapons and their armor, together with that basket covered in leather.
t.2.35.14: Seeing the two brothers mounted on the chariot with Sītā as the third, Sumantra boldly urged on the prized horses, equal in speed to the rush of the wind.
t.2.35.15: But when Rāghava had set out for the great forest for a long time, a swoon fell upon the city, and the people's strength gave way in a faint.
t.2.35.17: Then that city, sorely afflicted, together with its children and its old, ran toward Rāma alone, as one tormented by heat runs to water.
t.2.35.16: That city became filled with a great clamour, crowded and agitated, its elephants maddened and enraged, and resounding with the jingling and neighing of horses.
t.2.35.18: Clinging to him at his sides and from behind, their faces turned up toward him, all of them, their faces filled with tears and stricken with deep grief, spoke to him.
t.2.35.19: Rein in the horses, O charioteer, and go slowly, slowly. I will look upon Rāma's face, for soon it will be hard for us to see.
t.2.35.20: Surely, without doubt, the heart of Rāma's mother is made of iron, since it does not break when he, who is like a child of the gods, goes to the forest.
t.2.35.21: Vaidehī has indeed fulfilled her purpose, for, devoted to dharma, she follows her husband like his shadow and does not forsake him, just as the light of the sun does not forsake Mount Meru.
t.2.35.22: Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, you have attained your purpose, you who will serve your god-like brother, ever sweet of speech!
t.2.35.23: "Great indeed is this accomplishment of yours, and great is this rise in fortune; this is the very path to heaven, that you follow him." Speaking thus, they could not hold back the tears that came.
t.2.35.24: Then the king, dejected in mind and surrounded by sorrowful women, went forth from the palace, saying, "I shall see my beloved son."
t.2.35.25: And ahead was heard the loud clamor of weeping women, like the cry of she-elephants when a great tusker has been bound.
t.2.35.26: And his father, the glorious King Kākutstha, sunk in despair, then appeared like the full moon seized at its appointed time by the eclipsing planet.
t.2.35.27: Then, behind Rāma, there arose a cry of lamentation from the people, on seeing the king sinking down, deeply stricken with grief.
t.2.35.28: Some people cried, “Alas, Rāma!” and others, “Alas, mother of Rāma!”, and they lamented over the prosperous inner palace as it cried out in grief.
t.2.35.29: Rāma, looking back, saw the king, dejected and bewildered in mind, and his mother as well, both following him on the road. Bound by the noose of dharma, he did not look at them openly.
t.2.35.30: Seeing the two of them going on foot, they who deserved to ride in carriages, who did not deserve sorrow and were accustomed to comfort, he urged the charioteer, saying, “Drive quickly!”
t.2.35.31: For that tiger among men, like an elephant tormented by the goad, could not bear that painful sight of his father and his mother.
t.2.35.32: Then he looked back again and again at his mother Kausalyā, weeping thus and running after that chariot, crying out, "Rāma, Rāma! Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!", staggering as though she were dancing.
t.2.35.33: "Stop!" cried the king, while Rāghava urged, "Go on, go on!" And the heart of Sumantra was caught between the two, as if between the two wheels of a chariot.
t.2.35.34: "Even if you are reproached, you will tell the king, 'I did not hear.' To prolong sorrow is the most wicked thing," Rāma said to him.
t.2.35.35: Carrying out Rāma's word and taking leave of those people, the charioteer urged on the horses, though they were already going, to run swiftly.
t.2.35.36: The king's people turned back after reverently circling Rāma, yet in their minds and in their floods of tears they did not turn back from that man.
t.2.35.37: "One should not follow far the person whom one wishes to see return again": these words the ministers spoke to the great king Daśaratha.
t.2.35.38: Hearing their words, endowed with every virtue, the wretched king, his limbs bathed in sweat and his whole form sunk in dejection, stood there with his wife, gazing upon that son.
